what_this_is: An explicit model of the shape of shopper traffic, used to drive load tests. Every number below is an assumption drawn from published e-commerce norms, not from this shop. It is written down here, in one file, so the assumptions can be argued with and replaced rather than buried in a script.
how_to_replace_it: When the shop has real traffic, derive these from it: conversion from order counts over session counts, the query head/tail split from search logs, zero_result_share from the existing search_zero_result metric, and think time from session timestamps. Change the numbers, keep the shape, and set status to OBSERVED with the window the data came from.

session_mix.comment: What fraction of sessions get how far. The previous model converted 20% of sessions, which overstated write load by roughly ten times and would have made checkout look like the dominant cost.
session_mix.provenance: Published retail benchmarks put e-commerce conversion at roughly 1-3% of sessions and cart-add at roughly 3-5%. The midpoints are used. These are industry aggregates across very different shops and are the single least trustworthy numbers here.

query_distribution.comment: Search traffic is not uniform. A small head of popular queries serves most requests and is nearly always a cache hit; the long tail is where the retrieval cost actually is. A uniform query set measures neither.
query_distribution.provenance: Zipf-like head/tail is a well-established property of search traffic; the specific split is assumed.

query_quality.comment: Real search traffic is not clean. These rates exist so the benchmark exercises the fuzzy-matching and zero-result paths rather than only the happy one.
query_quality.provenance: Assumed. zero_result_share is the one that can be replaced first: search-service already exports a zero-result counter, so a day of real traffic settles it.

pacing.comment: Think time changes the concurrency shape at a given request rate. Without it, a journey completes instantly and the test holds far fewer sessions open than real traffic at the same RPS.
pacing.provenance: Assumed. A log-normal fits real dwell time better than uniform; uniform is used because fitting a shape nobody has measured adds false precision.

arrival.comment: Constant arrival rate is the right default for a capacity test because it does not hide degradation. Diurnal and burst profiles exist because they exercise autoscaling and cold caches, which a flat rate never does.

constant.description: Flat arrival rate. The default, and the only one to quote capacity from.

diurnal.description: A day compressed: trough, ramp, plateau, decay.

burst.description: A marketing send or a flash sale: a step change onto a cold cache.

shoppers.comment: distinct_shoppers models real isolation, where each shopper has their own cart. shared models the pathological case deliberately, to force contention on one cart. They answer different questions and must not be compared to each other.

limits: Every parameter here is assumed. None is derived from this shop.
Industry conversion aggregates span very different businesses; treat them as an order of magnitude, not a figure.
A model of the shape of traffic is not traffic. It cannot surface the queries nobody predicted, which is the main thing real traffic is worth.
